seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #13 — Build and Publish Your Package (2026)
altTitles: uv build, uv version and uv publish explained safely
seo.description: The final chapter of the uv course. uv build and why the wheel is built from the sdist, reading a wheel filename, --no-sources before publishing, uv version --bump with --dry-run, publishing to TestPyPI, trusted publishing, and verifying from a clean environment.

scenes.narration: Your code works. Now let anyone in the world install it with one command.

uv build, and two files appear in a folder called dist. Read the second line of that output carefully, because uv is saying something people get wrong constantly. Which of those two files does the other one come from? The wheel is built FROM the source distribution — not alongside it.

uvStage.headline: The wheel is built [from] the sdist
uvStage.premise: Two files in dist/, and the second is made out of the first. uv build says so.

stage.label: your project
stage.sub: the code as you wrote it

stage.label: invoice_app-0.1.0.tar.gz
stage.sub: the source, packaged

stage.label: invoice_app-...any.whl
stage.sub: the installable one

scenes.narration: Welcome back, and welcome to the last chapter. This one turns the project you've built into something anybody can install, and it does that without ever putting a secret on screen.

data.title: Ship it
data.subtitle: uv, chapter thirteen · build, version, publish

scenes.narration: Start with what those two files actually are, because they do different jobs.

A source distribution is your code, packed up. Anyone installing from an sdist has to build the package on their own machine first, which takes time and sometimes needs a compiler they haven't got. A wheel is the built result, ready to unpack straight into a folder — which is exactly why installing from a wheel is nearly instant.

uvStage.headline: One is [source]. One is built.
uvStage.premise: An sdist must be built on arrival. A wheel unpacks straight into place.

steps.label: tar tzf dist/invoice_app-0.1.0.tar.gz | head -3
steps.detail: the sdist is your project, as-is

stage.label: your project
stage.sub: what you wrote

stage.label: the sdist
stage.sub: must be built on arrival

stage.label: the wheel
stage.sub: unpacks straight into site-packages

scenes.narration: Reading the filename tells you a lot. Invoice underscore app is the package. Nought point one point zero is the version. Py three means any Python three. None means no C extensions. And any means any platform — which together say this wheel will install absolutely anywhere.

uvStage.headline: The filename is a [description]
uvStage.premise: Name, version, Python tag, ABI tag, platform tag. Five facts, in one filename.

steps.label: unzip -l dist/*.whl | head -3
steps.detail: and a wheel is only a zip file, inside

scenes.narration: Before publishing anything, two things need checking.

The first is easy to forget and embarrassing to get wrong. If your project points at a local folder or a git branch while you're developing, that pointer must not travel into the published package, because nobody else has your folder. Building with no-sources makes uv resolve exactly as a stranger would.

uvStage.headline: Build as a [stranger] would
uvStage.premise: A local path or a git branch works on your machine and nowhere else.

steps.label: uv build --no-sources
out: Caused by: not found in the package registry
steps.detail: caught here, instead of by a stranger

stage.label: on your machine
stage.sub: resolved from ../shared-utils

stage.label: for anyone else
stage.sub: no such folder exists

scenes.narration: The second is the version number, and uv manages that for you. uv version prints the current one. Bump takes it forward by major, minor or patch. Dry-run shows you the arrow without changing a single file, which is the safest way to check the bump does what you meant.

uvStage.headline: Bump it, but [look] first
uvStage.premise: --dry-run prints the change as an arrow and writes nothing at all.

scenes.narration: A quick word on what those three words mean, because choosing wrongly annoys everybody downstream. Patch is a fix that breaks nothing. Minor adds something new while keeping everything that already worked working. Major means you broke something deliberately, and every person depending on your package now has to read the release notes.

uvStage.headline: Major, minor, [patch]
uvStage.premise: The number is a promise to everyone who depends on you. Choose it honestly.

steps.label: uv version --bump patch --dry-run
steps.detail: a fix, and nothing else changed

scenes.narration: And now publishing — carefully, because this is the step involving credentials.

uv publish uploads what's in dist. Authentication comes from an environment variable, and I want to be explicit here: you set that variable in your own shell, and it never appears in a command, in a file, or on anybody's screen. What you see here is the variable's name, never its contents.

uvStage.headline: The token is a [variable name]
uvStage.premise: Set it in your own shell. It belongs in no command, no file, and no recording.

steps.label: echo "${UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN:+set}"
steps.detail: confirms it exists without printing it

stage.label: the variable name
stage.sub: UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN, shown freely

stage.label: the value
stage.sub: not in a command, a file, or a video

scenes.narration: Practise on TestPyPI first. It's a completely separate copy of the index, built for exactly this, and a mistake there costs nothing at all. Point publish at it with the index flag, and you get the whole experience without touching the real thing.

uvStage.headline: Practise on [TestPyPI] first
uvStage.premise: A separate index, built for rehearsal. A mistake there costs you nothing.

steps.label: uv publish --index testpypi
steps.detail: the real experience, on a practice index

stage.label: TestPyPI
stage.sub: wipe it, redo it, nobody minds

stage.label: PyPI
stage.sub: a published version cannot be replaced

stage.label: uv publish
stage.sub: and the same command does both

scenes.narration: There's a better option than a token, if you publish from a repository. Trusted publishing lets your CI provider prove who it is directly to the index, which means no token is created, stored or rotated — and a secret that doesn't exist cannot leak.

uvStage.headline: Better: [no] credential at all
uvStage.premise: Trusted publishing proves identity directly. There is no secret to store or leak.

steps.label: uv publish
steps.detail: no token was set, or needed

stage.label: with a token
stage.sub: created, stored, rotated, and leakable

stage.label: trusted publishing
stage.sub: nothing to store, so nothing to leak

scenes.narration: Then verify, because publishing is not the same as working. Run your package from a completely clean environment, with no project around it at all. If the import succeeds under those conditions, a stranger with nothing on their machine can install what you published.

uvStage.headline: Prove it from [nothing]
uvStage.premise: A clean environment, no project, straight from the index. That is the real test.

steps.label: uv run --with invoice-app --no-project -- \
steps.detail: a fresh environment, no project at all

steps.label: python -c "import invoice_app; print('ok')"
steps.detail: and a stranger would get exactly this

scenes.narration: Two build flags are worth knowing before you need them. You can build only the wheel, or only the sdist, which matters in a build pipeline where the two are produced by different jobs. You can also build a package that lives in a subfolder of a larger repository.

uvStage.headline: Build [one], or the other
uvStage.premise: Separate flags for each artefact, and a path for a package inside a bigger repo.

stage.label: packages/parser
stage.sub: one package inside a larger repo

stage.label: --sdist only
stage.sub: when a later job builds the wheel

stage.label: --wheel only
stage.sub: when the sdist already exists

scenes.narration: One rule about published versions catches people badly, so let me say it plainly. A version, once published, is permanent. You cannot re-upload nought point two point zero with different contents, ever. If you got it wrong, the fix is always to publish a new version — never to try to replace an old one.

uvStage.headline: A published version is [permanent]
uvStage.premise: You cannot re-upload a version with different contents. The fix is a new number.

stage.label: invoice-app
stage.sub: published, and now permanent

stage.label: invoice-app
stage.sub: the only real fix there is

scenes.narration: One last thought, for whoever installs what you publish. Everything from chapter nine applies to your users as well: their lockfile records the exact bytes of your wheel. So the more carefully you version, the less painful your package becomes to depend on.

uvStage.headline: They lock [you], too
uvStage.premise: Whoever installs your package records its exact bytes, just as you record theirs.
uvStage.stageTitle: the other side of chapter nine

steps.label: uv add invoice-app && grep -A2 invoice uv.lock
steps.detail: your package, sealed into their lockfile

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: and yours sits in the list like any other

scenes.narration: Last quiz of the course. What does uv build with no-sources actually protect you from? Pause the video here and think it through before I answer. Ready? From publishing something that only resolves on your own machine, because of a local path.

quiz.question: What does uv build --no-sources protect you from?
quiz.why: A local path resolves on your machine and nowhere else at all.

scenes.narration: So that's the whole course. You started with a shelf that everything fought over. You now have a project with its own shelf, an exact list of what's on it, a Python version pinned to it, and a package anybody in the world can install. Thirteen chapters, and no ritual to remember.

uvStage.headline: From one shelf, to [shipped]
uvStage.premise: Everything the course built, in the order it was built, and none of it manual.

steps.label: uv init && uv add rich && uv build && uv publish

stage.label: uv
stage.sub: and none of it was yours to remember

scenes.narration: So, to recap. uv build writes a source distribution and then builds the wheel out of it. Build with no-sources before publishing, so a local path can't escape into the world. And keep every credential in an environment variable, where nobody can read it over your shoulder.

points.text: The wheel is built FROM the sdist
Tokens live in the environment, not on screen

scenes.narration: That's the course. Go and make something, and if it helped, the whole series is right here waiting for the next person who needs it.
